front.title: Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) Transport over QUIC

abstract.t: This document specifies how an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) session is mapped onto a QUIC connection. EPP over QUIC (EoQ) leverages features of the QUIC protocol.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This document specifies how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) is mapped onto QUIC transport . QUIC is a protocol that is based on UDP and incorporates encryption support using TLS . Though based on UDP, QUIC provides connection semantics like other stateful protocols. This document discusses how EPP implementations can work with this and other features of QUIC while preserving the core EPP semantics.

EPP sessions use a single QUIC stream for all command and response exchanges throughout the session lifecycle.
Unlike stateless transaction protocols that permit per-command independent streams, EPP is a stateful protocol
with inherent sequential command dependencies defined in .
Maintaining a single stream preserves ordered transaction processing, consistent session state,
and full compatibility with existing EPP operational and implementation models.

EPP was designed for pluggability of transports that must follow . EoQ defines a fully pluggable QUIC transport for EPP as an alternative to other EPP transports, such as EPP over TCP (EoT) . The server can choose to offer EoQ in addition to EoT or as a replacement for EoT, based on the security and performance considerations of QUIC and the preferred deployment architecture of the server and clients.

EPP is primarily deployed for communication between domain registries
and registrars, which commonly run many concurrent EPP sessions.
Conventional EPP over TCP (EoT) requires a dedicated TCP connection
for every single EPP session, resulting in connection
overhead and resource consumption. EoQ addresses this issue by
leveraging QUIC stream multiplexing: multiple independent EPP
sessions can run over one single persistent QUIC connection.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document makes use of the following terms:

dd.t: The acronym used for the EPP-over-QUIC transport that defines the use of QUIC as an EPP transport following the considerations in .

Is a client-initiated bidirectional QUIC stream established on a QUIC connection using the "EoQ" Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) value. The EoQ connection maps to the client-server connection defined in , where the server returns an EPP <greeting>. A single QUIC connection supports many EoQ connections.
Is an authenticated EoQ connection, which occurs after a successful EPP <login>.

Used by clients to complete the creation of an EoQ connection by signaling the server to create the QUIC stream and return the EPP <greeting> needed for an EPP connection. formally defines the EoQ Connection Start Packet.

section.name: Session Management
section.t: Mapping EPP session management facilities onto the QUIC service is accomplished with a combination of a QUIC connection with the "EoQ" ALPN value and client-initiated, bidirectional QUIC streams. QUIC supports four stream types (), but EoQ only supports the client-initiated, bidirectional stream type.

As shown in , an EPP session first requires creation of a QUIC connection between two peers, one that initiates the connection request and one that responds to the connection request. The initiating peer is called the "client", and the responding peer is called the "server". By default, an EPP server MUST listen for QUIC connection requests on the well-known UDP port number updated by IANA (see ), unless there is a mutual agreement to use another port number.
A successfully established QUIC connection is secured by the TLS support that QUIC provides using the "EoQ" ALPN value.

Once the QUIC connection is established, the EPP client MUST then create a bidirectional QUIC stream by sending the EoQ Connection Start Packet. states that "streams can be created by sending data". If the EPP server accepts the QUIC stream, it reads the EoQ Connection Start Packet and returns an EPP <greeting> to the client on the same QUIC stream. After reading the EPP <greeting> message, and absent processing errors, the EPP client sends EPP commands and receives EPP responses on the same stream. A QUIC stream corresponds to an EPP connection, which is referred to as an EoQ connection. An authenticated QUIC stream, via a successful EPP <login>, corresponds to an EPP session, which is referred to as an EoQ session.

An EPP session is normally ended by the client issuing an EPP <logout> command. A server receiving an EPP <logout> command MUST end the EPP session and close the QUIC stream. A client MAY end an EoQ session by closing the QUIC stream and the server MUST end the EoQ session by closing the QUIC stream.
EoQ connections are established as described in the QUIC transport specification . During connection establishment, EoQ support is indicated using the "EoQ" ALPN value in the cryptographic handshake.

A single QUIC connection may allow multiple QUIC streams. This means that a single QUIC connection may support multiple EoQ sessions. A server MAY limit the life span of an established EoQ session. EoQ sessions that are inactive for more than a server-defined period MAY be ended by the server closing the QUIC stream. A server MAY close EoQ sessions that have been open and active for longer than a server-defined limit.
The max_idle_timeout transport parameter defined in MUST NOT be set to a non-zero value by the client or server. Once the last QUIC stream for a QUIC connection is closed, the server MAY either immediately end the QUIC connection or retain the open connection in accordance with local configuration and operational policy.

section.name: Message Exchange
section.t:
EPP messages are passed on an EoQ connection, which is a client-initiated, bidirectional QUIC stream, defined in .
Except for the EPP server <greeting>, EPP messages are initiated by the EPP client in the form of EPP commands. An EPP server MUST return an EPP response to an EPP command on the same QUIC stream that carried the command. If the QUIC stream is closed after a server receives and successfully processes a command but before the response can be returned to the client, the server MAY attempt to undo the effects of the command to ensure a consistent state between the client and the server. EPP commands are idempotent, so processing a command more than once produces the same net effect on the repository as successfully processing the command once.

An EPP client streams EPP commands to an EPP server on an established QUIC stream. A client MAY establish multiple QUIC streams to support multiple EoQ sessions with each EoQ session mapped to a single QUIC stream.
A server SHOULD limit a client to a maximum number of QUIC streams per QUIC connection based on server capabilities and operational load. Absent such a limit, a server may be subject to overload and resource exhaustion. discusses this situation.
EPP describes client-server interaction as a command-response exchange where the client sends one command to the server and the server returns one response to the client.
Each EPP data unit MUST contain a single EPP message. Commands MUST be processed independently.

A server SHOULD impose a limit on the amount of time required for a client to issue a well-formed EPP command to reduce the risk associated with a resource exhaustion attack. For example, the time limit is 10 minutes for the server idle timeout and 8 minutes for client keep-alive.
Absent local policy, a server MUST end an EoQ session and close the QUIC stream if a well-formed command is not received within the time limit.

A general state machine for an EPP server is described in . A general client-server message exchange using QUIC transport is illustrated in .
It shows an example of successful exchange over a single QUIC stream of a QUIC connection.
Many QUIC streams may be opened and closed during the life of a QUIC connection.

section.name: Data Unit Format
section.t:
The EPP data unit contains two fields: a 32-bit header that describes the total length of the data unit, and the EPP XML instance. The length of the EPP XML instance is determined by subtracting four octets from the total length of the data unit. A receiver must successfully read that many octets to retrieve the complete EPP XML instance before processing the EPP message.
The EPP data unit format is depicted in (one tick mark represents one bit position).
The fields shown in are defined as follows:

dd.t: The total length of the EPP data unit measured in octets in network (big endian) byte order. The octets contained in this field MUST be included in the total length calculation. The 32-bit total length matches the total length used in EoT, defined in , to support transport pluggability.

dl.dd: The EPP XML instance carried in the data unit.

section.name: EoQ Connection Start Packet
section.t: The EoQ Connection Start Packet is written by the client after creating a QUIC stream to signal to the server to initialize the QUIC stream. Absent processing errors or local policy, the server accepts the QUIC stream, reads the EoQ Connection Start Packet, and returns the EPP <greeting> to the client on same QUIC stream.

The EoQ Connection Start Packet follows the Data Unit Format with two fields: a 32-bit header that describes the total length of the data unit, and the constant value of "EoQ Connection Start" instead of an "EPP XML Instance". The length of a valid data unit MUST be 24 octets, which includes 4 octets for the Total Length and 20 octets for the "EoQ Connection Start" constant value.

If the EoQ Connection Start Packet received by the server is not valid (e.g., when the total length is not exactly 24 octets), the server MUST close that QUIC stream. The server MAY return an error indication prior to closing the stream.

section.name: Transport Considerations
section.t: describes considerations to be addressed by protocol transport mappings. This document addresses each of those considerations using a combination of features of the QUIC protocol and features of this document as discussed below:

dl.dd: QUIC guarantees ordered processing of data within each stream. describes streams in detail.
EPP session management utilizes QUIC streams and is described in .

QUIC supports stateful communications between endpoints via Connection IDs and long-lived streams within each connection. QUIC streams on top of QUIC connections, defined in Sections and of , are used to create stateful communications between the client and server.
EoQ uses the packet framing defined in .
QUIC provides various mechanisms to help achieve congestion avoidance. describes these mechanisms in detail.
QUIC uses message acknowledgement, packet retransmission, and other features to ensure reliability. describes these features in detail.

dd.t: Pipelining is allowed in EoQ. QUIC streams support sending multiple frames without waiting for responses from the other peer. This does not change the basic single command, single response operating mode of the core EPP.
Commands MUST be processed independently and in the same order as sent from the client.
Batch-oriented processing (combining multiple EPP commands in a single data unit) is not permitted. Each EPP data unit must contain a single EPP message.

An EPP x5zz "Connection Management" error response, defined in , of a well-formed EPP client packet results in the server closing the EoQ connection after returning the error response. A malformed EPP client packet results in the server closing the EoQ connection without providing an error response. All subsequent EPP commands sent on the EoQ connection will not be processed.

section.name: Operational Considerations
section.t: Some of the concerns examined within this section are also addressed in . Authors of this specification encourage implementers to understand .

section.name: Clients Fall Back with Management of Multiple Transport
section.t: If the establishment of an EoQ connection fails, clients MAY attempt to fall back to EPP over TCP as specified in , depending on local deployment and security policy. It is up to clients to determine the mix of transports that best meets their business needs.

section.name: Port Number Reuse
section.t:
Although does only a request for TCP, the companion UDP port number was also allocated. That practice was prior to when TCP and UDP port numbers were simultaneously assigned when either was requested.
updates EPP UDP/700 allocation to be used exclusively for EoQ. This update does not introduce any operational issues given that there are no known implementations of EPP over UDP.

section.name: QUIC Support Announcement and Discovery
section.t: There is no dedicated in-band mechanism defined in this specification for a server to explicitly announce EoQ support to clients. Operators MAY use out-of-band configuration or provisioning channels to advertise server EoQ support to clients in advance.

section.name: Configuration Parameters
section.t:
Implementations MAY configure operational parameters to control EoQ session behavior. These parameters can include idle session timeout, maximum QUIC streams per connection, command processing timeout, and maximum session timeout.
Servers and clients SHOULD configure limits to avoid session disruption and resource exhaustion.

aside.t: Implementation Note: There is no in-band protocol mechanism to align limits. Operators typically distribute standard settings via SDKs. Client timeout and stream limits shall be set lower than server values for graceful connection handling. Timeout rules are consistent across EoT and EoQ; per-connection stream limits are newly introduced in EoQ.

section.name: Diagnostic and Troubleshooting
section.t: Operators SHOULD log the EoQ connection establishment status, stream lifecycle events, and command transaction results for diagnostic purposes. QUIC transport errors and EPP protocol failures ought to be distinguishable to facilitate efficient troubleshooting. Implementations MAY provide granular error reporting to help identify session termination, connection timeout, and stream closure root causes. Operators MUST redact sensitive data in the logs, such as user credentials and authorization information values.

section.name: Address Validation
section.t: EoQ implementations MUST follow the address validation requirements defined in to mitigate potential amplification attacks and validate client address reachability.

section.name: Authentication Considerations
section.t: EoQ relies on the TLS authentication mechanisms defined in for peer authentication and credential validation. Implementations MUST follow the same authentication practices specified for EPP over TLS in . Server and client authentication procedures remain unchanged from existing EPP deployment models when running over QUIC transport.

section.name: 0-RTT and Session Resumption
section.t: Using 0-RTT for EoQ allows clients to establish connections and initiate EPP transactions without round-trip delay, enabling servers to use shorter idle timers and reduce connection overhead. Session resumption and 0-RTT introduce privacy and replay risks.

EPP commands fall into three categories: session management, queries, and transform commands. EPP query commands perform read-only object information retrieval operations. Only read-only EPP query commands MAY be carried in 0-RTT STREAM frames; all other EPP commands MUST NOT use 0-RTT.
Clients SHOULD use resumption tickets only once specified in . Servers SHOULD issue session-resumption tickets with a sufficiently long lifetime (e.g., 6 hours). Servers SHOULD implement the anti-replay mechanisms specified in .
EoQ implementations SHOULD follow the guidance in and to balance performance and risk mitigation. Failure to do so increases privacy exposure and replay attack risks.

section.name: Registration of an EoQ Identification String
section.t: This document creates a new registration for the identification of EoQ in the "TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) Protocol IDs" registry under the "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions" registry group available at .

section.name: Registration of Port Number
section.t: The "Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry" () contains an entry for EPP UDP/700. However, there is no known usage of EPP over UDP. This document therefore specifies EPP over UDP as defined here. IANA has updated the description field of the EPP UDP/700 entry to be "EPP running over QUIC" and added this document as an additional reference alongside .

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t:
EPP over QUIC provides similar security foundations as EPP over TCP with TLS, though the security properties of QUIC specified in differ from those of TLS/TCP in that QUIC is an encrypted transport protocol.
Some related security issues are discussed in and . Sections and of this document also discuss related security issues.

EoQ servers run the risk of a resource exhaustion attack by allowing the creation of unlimited QUIC streams per QUIC connection. As indicated in ,
servers should limit a client to a maximum number of QUIC streams per QUIC connection based on server capabilities and operational load. Absent such a limit, the server may be subject to overload that would exhaust its resources.

The 32-bit total length field defined in allows a declared payload size up to approximately 4 gigabytes. Implementations MUST validate the advertised total length against a locally configured maximum frame size limit before allocating memory or attempting to read the full frame. Without this check, an attacker could send a crafted frame with an excessively large length value to exhaust receiver memory and trigger a denial-of-service condition.
